ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.title: Unpaid Land Compensation on the Coastal Embankment Polders

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-52800 for the First Phase of the Coastal Embankment Improvement Project (P128276). US$375 million approved 26 June 2013. The credit disbursed US$311.84 million. Original closing was 31 December 2020; actual closing was 31 December 2023. The original total project cost of US$400 million was cut to US$375.74 million after US$24.26 million of the credit, or SDR 18.2 million, was cancelled 17 days before closing. The scope was cut from 17 polders to 10 in January 2020. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the Bangladesh Water Development Board. The project financed land acquisition and the resettlement and rehabilitation of people adversely affected by it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024; IEG ICR Review ICRR0024220, 30 November 2024).

lenders.name: Pilot Program for Climate Resilience, Strategic Climate Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-14713 of US$25 million alongside the IDA credit; US$24,999,892.29 disbursed. Total disbursement across the credit and the grant was US$336.84 million as of 15 May 2024 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024).

ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.community: The project raised and widened embankments around coastal polders, which required private land and moved people living on the existing embankments. At appraisal the census survey of February 2012 found the first works package alone would affect 6,203 households and persons in their homes, places of business and other assets, plus 184 common resource structures, most of them on the existing embankments. Land acquisition and compensation ran years behind the works. The completion report records that as of April 2024, four months after the credit closed, land acquisition payment stood at 92.4 per cent. The ICR Review adds that the Bank task team put the figure at 94 per cent as of June 2024 and that there was no further update after that. The unpaid balance was attributed to incomplete embankment works, compensation amounts as small as BDT 345, about US$4.00, and missing proof of ownership, including unavailable mauza maps, khatians, transfer and succession documents and possession records, as well as disputed claims and parcels under court cases. Responsibility for finishing the payments was left after closing to the project's key focal point, the Bangladesh Water Development Board's operation and maintenance engineers and the Deputy Commissioner offices of the districts concerned. The ICR Review notes that the interim government changed the district administrations, including the Deputy Commissioners responsible for land acquisition payment, several times. Under the first works package 291 female-headed households were affected by resettlement and under the second works package 478; the completion report says the women heading those households received relocation and resettlement benefits and a grant. Thirty-six grievance redress committees were set up across the first two packages and received 269 complaints by 31 December 2023, all of which were closed. The completion report also states that resettlement assistance for involuntarily displaced people without title was completed before works started on each section. Financial management shortcomings forfeited US$12.69 million of concessional IDA funding, made up of US$6.24 million from an undocumented designated account and US$6.45 million left undisbursed.
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,325 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figure in the Bank's own documents is the appraisal count of 6,203 households and persons affected in the first works package, from the February 2012 census survey in the Project Appraisal Document. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2023 with land acquisition payment incomplete. The Bank task team reported 94 per cent paid as of June 2024 and the ICR Review, published 30 November 2024, records no update after that date. The outcome was rated Moderately Satisfactory on a split rating.

ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.confidence_note: The lending terms, the payment percentages and their dates, and the appraisal affected-household count all come from the Bank's own completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it and the appraisal document. What is thin is the people: no document found names the households still unpaid, says how many they are, or gives a count of people actually relocated. The 92.4 and 94 per cent figures are percentages of payment value or of parcels, which the documents do not define.

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.point: Wazir Khan Mosque on the Shahi Guzargah, the historic street the works ran along (OpenStreetMap point for the mosque)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan L7380-PK for the Punjab Municipal Services Improvement Project (P083929). US$50 million approved 1 June 2006, loan agreement signed 5 June 2006; US$48.85 million disbursed against total project costs of US$54.59 million, compared with US$59.00 million at appraisal. Closing was extended twice, by 23 months in the August 2010 restructuring and by a further 12 months to 30 November 2013. Component 2 financed the pilot works in the Walled City of Lahore, including the Resettlement Action Plan. Outcome and overall Bank performance were both rated Moderately Satisfactory, and risk to development outcome Significant (IEG ICR Review ICRR14661, 2 June 2015; World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 May 2014).

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.community: The project paid for the first stage of rebuilding the Shahi Guzargah, a 1.6 km historic street through the Walled City of Lahore, together with the facades, street surfacing, water supply, sewerage, drainage and electrical network along it. Surveys for the Resettlement Action Plan found 147 shops, counting sub-units, that had to be removed completely, 732 more shops that would be affected temporarily along the Shahi Guzargah, and 264 encroachments onto public space, mainly kitchens and washrooms, in the 47 residential streets running off it. The plan records who held the 147 shops: 84 belonged to the Auqaf Department, 22 to the Municipal Corporation, 18 to informal occupants and 10 were privately owned; 28 of the shopkeepers were owners, 76 non-resident owners, 8 resident tenants, 11 non-resident tenants and 22 were in an 'others' category. It also counted 79 day-seller shops, 10 khokhas (kiosks), 2 tharas and 19 mixed cases among the temporary sellers who would have to be compensated, and 53 employees working in the shops. Of the 147 shopkeepers, 50 were earning between Rs 5,000 and Rs 20,000 a month and 61 between Rs 21,000 and Rs 35,000. Payments were to be made by cross cheque through the Revenue Department, to people with documentary proof of ownership. Employees of permanently displaced shops were to get a one-off Rs 15,000 and employees of temporarily disturbed shops Rs 6,000. By closing, the completion report records that 147 shops and 264 encroachments had been removed and 732 shops had been given temporary support, after more than a thousand meetings with shopkeepers, traders and residents. At closing the facade work was 72 per cent complete and street surfacing 52 per cent, with the rest finished using Government of Punjab funds.
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,153 for this project. That figure is the plan-stage estimate in the Resettlement Action Plan itself, which states: 'Based on 879 shops/owners of the property being affected from minor to severe degrees with average family size of 7 persons, there would be impact on 6153 persons due to the project implementation in the Pilot Project area.' It is an estimate of people affected, arrived at by multiplying affected shops by an assumed household size, and not a count of people moved. The plan separately counted 371 people in the families of the 53 shop employees.
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.outcome: The loan closed on 30 November 2013 with the street works unfinished and completed afterwards with provincial funds. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the resettlement work a successful pilot. No independent follow-up study of what happened to the 147 shopkeepers after removal was found.

What is thin is the aftermath: no document found records how much was actually paid to the 147 shopkeepers or the 53 employees, whether any were relocated to new premises, or what their incomes were afterwards. lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits and grants IDA-48320, IDA-50020, IDA-58650, IDA-H3390 and IDA-H6290 for the Road Sector Development Project (P095977). US$42.6 million approved 6 December 2007, raised through additional financing to a revised commitment of US$128,515,589.07, of which US$126,444,070 was disbursed; total project cost US$126,444,070. Original closing was 30 June 2012; actual closing was 15 January 2020. Category B. The implementing agency was the Department of Roads. The project carried out a programme of compensation, resettlement and rehabilitation of displaced persons. Social and environmental safeguards compliance was rated Moderately Satisfactory at the last implementation support mission in November and December 2019; monitoring and evaluation quality was rated Modest (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2020; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022396, 22 February 2021).

companies.name: Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats Pvt. Ltd.
companies.role: Indian consulting firm that prepared the detailed survey and design and the Resettlement Action Plan for the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road under the project's Phase I, in association with Nepali firms (Resettlement Action Plan, September 2007).

companies.name: Full Bright Consultancy (Pvt.) Ltd.
companies.role: Nepali consultancy, in joint venture with Soil Test (P) Ltd and Himal Integrated Consultancy (P) Ltd, associated in preparing the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road survey, design and Resettlement Action Plan (Resettlement Action Plan, September 2007).

nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.community: The project upgraded dry-season roads and tracks to all-season standard and maintained highway and feeder roads, scaled up from about 297 km to 700 km of upgrading. Its social impacts were land acquisition leading to involuntary resettlement, loss of strips of land, loss of structures, disturbance and disruption of livelihoods, and loss of common property resources. The completion report accounts for 115 project-affected households in total. Cash compensation was paid in full to 91 of them for 76 land parcels and 48 structures. For the remaining 24 households, holding 19 land parcels and 11 structures, compensation was still outstanding at closing because the households had not supplied the documents and clearance needed for payment. The money for 22 of those 24 households had been deposited at their district administration offices; for the other two, payment awaited a determination by the Compensation Determining Committee, after which the Department of Roads was to place the amount in an escrow account. Financial management was downgraded to moderately unsatisfactory in 2018-19, partly over non-compliance with contract terms on a 5 per cent mobilisation advance. One road under the project, Satbanjh-Jhulaghat, had its own Resettlement Action Plan in September 2007, which counted 73 affected households on that road alone, of which 7 were severely affected and about 5 were Dalit households among the vulnerable groups.
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,824 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report accounts for 115 project-affected households in all, and the one road-level resettlement plan opened here counts 73 affected households on the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.outcome: The credit closed on 15 January 2020 with compensation unpaid to 24 households. The completion report leaves the final payments to the district administration offices and the Compensation Determining Committee, and no later document found records whether they were made.

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.title: Land and Structures Taken for the Swat Right-Bank Road
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.place: Provincial highway S3-B, Chakdara to Madyan on the right bank of the Swat river, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.point: Chakdara, the southern end of the reconstructed section of provincial highway S3-B (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank, as administrator of the Multi Donor Trust Fund for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan
lenders.role: Grants TF-10122, TF-15895 and TF-16992 for the MDTF KP Emergency Roads Recovery Project (P125584). Original commitment US$8.0 million, approved 23 August 2011 and effective 17 October 2011; first additional financing of US$9.1 million approved 15 January 2014 and second of US$9.0 million approved 30 May 2014; revised amount US$26.10 million and US$25.62 million disbursed. Closing ran from 30 June 2014 for the first phase to 31 October 2015 for the third. Category B. Trust fund money is not normally usable for compensation, so approval was sought and given to pay compensation for lost assets and lost production from the grant funds. Outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance were all rated Moderately Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 11 August 2016; IEG ICR Review, 28 February 2017).

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.community: The project reconstructed 40.9 km of provincial highway S3-B from Chakdara towards Madyan on the right bank of the Swat river, plus link roads, after a military operation and floods. The road serves a population of about 300,000 people on the right bank. The project paper for the first phase estimated that 498 people would be directly affected, about 3.75 acres of land would be acquired with crop-loss compensation on a further 1.75 acres where farmers had encroached on the right of way, 1,000 trees would be lost and 158 structures affected. The completion report gives the outcome: in Phase I, 114 people were affected, 1.6 acres of land in all were acquired or reclaimed, 74 trees were lost and 24 structures. In Phase II, 88 people were affected, crops were lost over 4.5 acres, and 731 trees and 23 structures were lost. In Phase III, 12 people were affected with very small losses. That is 214 affected people across the three phases. The completion report states that 98 per cent of affected parties had been compensated by the time it was written; the remainder were absent and had not responded to efforts to reach them. It also records delays in compensation payment at times, and says that when the provincial highway authority pulled its Deputy Director for Environment and Resettlement out of the project management unit for five months there were delays in handling grievance cases and in paying compensation. The report adds that the provincial government appears reluctant to devote staff and resources to social and environmental compliance. Grievance redress committees made up of affected people dealt with disputes over land ownership, compensation and payment delays.
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,398 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 214 people affected across the three phases and 498 estimated for Phase I at the project-paper stage. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.killed_note: Two suicide attacks occurred while the project was being implemented, according to the completion report, which gives them as a cause of delay and does not attribute them to the project, its contractors or anyone acting for them, and does not say whether anyone was killed.
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.outcome: The last grant closed on 31 October 2015 with 2 per cent of affected parties uncompensated because they could not be found. The project's savings on compensation and land acquisition, which came in below the amounts provided for, were used to build additional lengths of road.

sources.title: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Emergency Road Recovery Project (P125584)
Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, PK: KP Emergency Roads Recovery Project (P125584)

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.confidence_note: The affected-person counts, acreages, tree and structure counts and the 98 per cent compensation figure come from the Bank's own completion report, and are unusually specific. What is thin is that the harm is small in scale and partly self-reported by the implementing agency; the report names no affected person, gives no compensation rate, and does not say how long the payment delays ran. The 2 per cent left uncompensated is not converted into a number of people.

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.title: Land and Structures Lost to the Siddhirganj Gas Pipeline and Transmission Line
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.place: Siddhirganj power plant, Narayanganj, with the gas pipeline from Bakhrabad through Cumilla and Narayanganj districts and the transmission line through Konapara and Demra, Bangladesh
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.point: The Electricity Generation Company of Bangladesh plant site at Siddhirganj, the project's generating site (OpenStreetMap industrial point named for the EGCB plant)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-45080 and IDA-57370 for the Siddhirganj Power Project, originally the Siddhirganj Peaking Power Project (P095965). IDA-45080: US$350 million approved 30 October 2008, effective 31 March 2009, revised to US$332,621,020 and US$309,875,467 disbursed. IDA-57370: US$176,710,000, revised to US$115,501,477 and US$112,652,157 disbursed. Total Bank financing US$526,710,000 original, US$422,527,624 disbursed. The borrower's planned contribution of US$312,890,000 is recorded as nil disbursed. Original closing 31 March 2016; actual closing 31 December 2019. Environmental category A, full assessment. Outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory. The completion report notes that the resettlement and rehabilitation costs under the gas transmission and power grid components were not financed by the World Bank (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Gas Transmission Company Limited (GTCL)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the gas pipeline component and, through a contracted organisation, paid compensation to the people affected by it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (PGCB)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the transmission line component and changed the line route after objections; unable under government rules to acquire private land permanently, it paid only crop and temporary-loss compensation to private landowners (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Electricity Generation Company of Bangladesh (EGCB)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the power station, signed the engineering, procurement and construction contracts with a joint-venture consortium the completion report does not name, and built the replacement school building (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: NTPC Limited
companies.role: Government of India enterprise that holds the operation and maintenance contract for the plant, concluded with EGCB (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Development Organization for the Rural Poor (DORP)
companies.role: Organisation engaged to carry out the resettlement of the people affected by the gas pipeline and to deliver GTCL's compensation to them (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.community: The project built a power station at Siddhirganj, a gas pipeline to feed it and a transmission line to carry its output. The gas pipeline required permanent acquisition of 46.05 hectares of land and temporary requisition of 85.00 hectares along the alignment. The completion report records 1,501 entitled people affected by the project; 93 of them lost structures, one lost a poultry farm and one lost a pond, and 201 female-headed households were affected. People losing roughly 20 per cent or more of their assets were treated as vulnerable and put into a livelihood restoration programme of cash grants and skills training. Handover of the pipeline right of way was itself delayed: the Narayanganj and Cumilla district administrations began handing over land only in mid-May 2012. On the transmission line, people living on the planned right of way objected to the route because of its impact in dense residential areas. The line was moved. The old route would have affected 72 families on private and public land; the route chosen instead affected 19 families, most of them squatting on public land and on private agricultural or industrial land. Because government rules barred the power grid company from permanently acquiring private land, the private landowners on the line were not compensated for their land at all. They kept ownership and received only compensation for crops and related temporary losses during construction. Across the grid and pipeline works the completion report says over 20,000 project-affected households were compensated for permanent and temporary impacts to land, land use and crops or livelihoods. Noise and emissions from the plant were found to put a nearby school and its students at risk, and a new school building was built at a safe distance and handed to the Bangladesh Power Development Board.
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,444 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 1,501 entitled people affected by the gas pipeline and 19 families affected by the transmission line route that was built, against 72 families on the route that was dropped. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2019. The transmission line was rerouted after objections, cutting the families affected from 72 to 19. Private landowners along the line retained title but were never paid for the land itself. Resettlement and rehabilitation costs on the pipeline and grid components were borne outside the Bank's financing.

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.confidence_note: The hectares, the 1,501 entitled people, the 93 who lost structures, the 201 female-headed households and the statement that private landowners were not compensated for their land all come from the Bank's own completion report. What is thin is who those people are and where: the report gives no village names beyond Siddhirganj-Konapara in Demra for the transmission line, does not say what the 19 families on the chosen route lost, and does not break the 'over 20,000 households' figure down or say what each was paid. The joint-venture consortium that built the plant is not named in any document opened.

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.title: Two-Year Gap Between Land Taking and Compensation on the Gujarat Highways
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.place: Eight road widening corridors in Gujarat, including Mehsana to Palanpur with the Mehsana bypass, Radhanpur to Chanasma and Vallabhipur to Ranghola, India
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.point: Mahesana (Mehsana) town, on the Mehsana-Palanpur corridor and the site of the 5 km Mehsana bypass added to the project (OpenStreetMap city point)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-83130 for the Second Gujarat State Highway Project (P114827). US$175 million approved 13 December 2013, loan agreement signed February 2014, and the full loan amount disbursed. Original closing 31 January 2019, extended by 23 months in the September 2018 restructuring; the project closed 31 December 2020. The borrower's contribution was US$158.50 million and the private sector's US$37.40 million. Component B financed land acquisition and resettlement, utility relocation and environmental management. Classified Category A and triggered the Bank's policies on involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, forests and physical cultural resources (IEG ICR Review, 13 June 2022; World Bank Project Appraisal Document, 7 November 2013).

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.community: The project widened and strengthened eight road corridors and rehabilitated three more added in 2018. At appraisal the social impact assessments found that about 730 project-affected households, title holders and non-title holders together, 23 hectares of private land, 7 hectares of government land and 304 privately owned structures, mostly shops, would be affected by the widening and strengthening works. Three of the corridors passed through Schedule V areas with tribal populations, and three Scheduled Tribe households were recorded as affected. In the event, 14.4 hectares of land were acquired during implementation, of which 11.51 hectares were private. Acquisition in the eight corridors took two years. The notification of acquisition was issued in January 2017 under local law, but the notification awarding compensation could only be issued in February 2019 - a gap of about two years between the land being taken and the award of compensation being notified. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the completion report reports no issues with compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy, and that the lengthy land acquisition process delayed implementation and hurt the project's efficiency. District-level grievance redressal committees were set up to take complaints about resettlement and compensation, alongside postal correspondence and approaches to the executive engineers on site. Some religious structures affected by the works were relocated with the cooperation of local communities.
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,000 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of people in the documents opened is the appraisal estimate of about 730 project-affected households in the Project Appraisal Document, repeated in the ICR Review. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020 with the full US$175 million disbursed. No Implementation Completion and Results Report for this project appears in the Bank's document list; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, dated 13 June 2022, is the latest public account found.

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.confidence_note: The hectares acquired, the acquisition and compensation notification dates and the appraisal counts come from the Independent Evaluation Group's review and the appraisal document. dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.title: Dehlon Bypass Built Over a Disputed Plot, and Two Deaths on the Punjab Road Works
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.place: Dehlon bypass, Ludhiana district, Punjab, India
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.point: Dehlon town, Ludhiana district, where the bypass was built across the disputed plot (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-48430 for the Punjab State Road Sector Project (P090585). US$250 million approved 5 December 2006; US$248,110,727.51 disbursed against a total project cost of US$407.3 million. Original closing 5 June 2012; the project was restructured on 10 November 2014 and closed 5 June 2017, five years late. Environmental Category A, with the policies on environmental assessment, forests, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement triggered. The Bank team learned of two fatal workplace accidents only after asking the implementing board about them (IEG ICR Review, 8 May 2018; World Bank Project Appraisal Document, 10 November 2006).

dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.community: Two separate harms are on the record for this project. At Dehlon, where the project built a bypass, one of the owners of a plot refused the compensation offered in May 2017 and filed a case in the High Court; a complaint had already gone to the Bank's Grievance Redress Service in December 2016. In April 2017 the contractors tried to start work on the plot and the Bank team insisted all work stop until compensation was settled. Soon after the project closed on 5 June 2017 the contractor went back onto the plot and finished building the bypass. The Independent Evaluation Group records that half of the co-owners have been paid, that the co-owner who complained is still pursuing the matter in the High Court, and that the matter has not been resolved. Separately, two fatal workplace accidents happened on the project in 2016 and were not reported to the Bank; the Bank team found out about them only after making a specific request to the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board in February 2017, and then met contractors, consultants and the board about construction zone safety and traffic management. There was also a built harm from the drainage works: in 2009 the project team found that drains built in urban areas sat above the plinth level of the buildings next to them, blocking numerous commercial and residential entrances. The Independent Evaluation Group attributes this to weak monitoring and to the roads board's environment and social officers not being involved in two upgrading works, which were closed out without proper clean-up, rehabilitation or compliance reports. The Bank team later arranged an assessment and an action plan to remedy it. At appraisal the project expected 112 people from 24 households to be marginally or temporarily affected on the rehabilitation roads with none displaced, and on the upgrading roads 4,731 people affected at least temporarily, with people from 197 households expected to be displaced, and about 31 hectares of land to be acquired.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,977 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The appraisal document's own figure for people affected at least temporarily on the upgrading roads is 4,731, with 197 households expected to be displaced. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.killed_note: The two deaths counted are the two fatal workplace accidents on the project's works in 2016, which the Independent Evaluation Group's review records were not reported to the Bank and came to light only after the Bank asked the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board in February 2017. No document opened names the dead, gives the dates or locations of the accidents, says which contractor's works they occurred on, or records any compensation to their families.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.outcome: The loan closed on 5 June 2017. The bypass across the disputed plot was completed after closing. Half the co-owners have been paid; the co-owner who objected has not been, and the case continues in the High Court. The Independent Evaluation Group records the task team as still following the matter up as of its review of 8 May 2018. No later account was found.

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.title: Culvert 16/3 Drainage Dispute at Tudella, Ja-Ela
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.place: Culvert 16/3 on the A3 Colombo-Puttalam road near Gama Meda Road, Tudella, Ja-Ela, Gampaha District, Sri Lanka
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.point: Tudella, Ja-Ela, the locality the five people who filed the Inspection Panel request live in (OpenStreetMap point named Tudella on Agaradaguru Road)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-41380 (CR 4138-CE), IDA-44290 (CR 4429-CE) and IDA-49060 (CR 4906-LK) for the Road Sector Assistance Project (P086411) and its two additional financings. CR 4138-CE: US$100 million approved 15 December 2005, effective 16 March 2006, US$96.40 million disbursed. CR 4429-CE, first additional financing: US$98.10 million, 16 September 2008, US$83.60 million disbursed. CR 4906-LK, second additional financing (P116742): US$100 million, which the Inspection Panel notice dates to 29 April 2011 and the Panel's project information to 12 April 2011, US$75.00 million disbursed. Original total commitment XDR 69.10 million, revised and disbursed XDR 180.16 million, with XDR 12.14 million cancelled. Original closing 30 September 2011; actual closing 30 June 2015. Category B. Outcome rated Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome High. The implementing agency was the Road Development Authority under the Ministry of Ports and Highways (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2016; Inspection Panel Notice of Non-Registration, 10 November 2014).

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.community: On 24 March 2014 the World Bank Inspection Panel received a request for inspection, dated 25 February 2014, from five named people living in Tudella, Ja-Ela, near culvert 16/3 on the A3 Colombo-Puttalam road: M. J. R. Perera, M. N. D. Perera, Shirley Dias, Anthony Suriyarachchi and B. A. R. Mallika, writing for themselves and others. Their complaint concerned the rebuilt and enlarged culvert 16/3, financed by the project's second additional financing, which drains rainwater from the A3 into a private drain on Mr Perera's land. One of the requesters told the Panel that 67 individuals were affected by the handling of rainwater near the culvert and that about eight properties were likely to be hit. They said the enlarged culvert and the new side drains connected to it would push more water into the private drain than it could hold, worsening flooding that already happened in the area, and that the culvert channels water in the opposite direction to the natural slope of the land. On 26 January 2014 they closed the private trench permanently, in response to written requests and petitions from residents who feared flooding of houses on the opposite side of the street; Bank management told the Panel that this closure was in turn increasing flooding for neighbours elsewhere. The Road Development Authority offered to lay an underground hume pipe across Mr Perera's property in place of the open drain; he refused, treating construction on his land as a threat to his legal ownership and to the property's resale value, and Bank management found his own alternative not technically feasible for lack of elevation at the site. Mr Perera petitioned the Court of Appeal of Sri Lanka (C.A. Application No. 138/2014) over whether the drain on his land is private or public. The court granted an injunction halting construction on his property, and that injunction was still in force when the Panel wrote. On 10 November 2014 the Panel declined to register the request, because the question turned on the interpretation of local law, which is outside its mandate, and because, in the Panel's words, the likelihood of harm from possible flooding potentially exacerbated by the project was not occurring at that time. Separately, the completion report records that the project received over 4,000 public complaints, all but two of which were resolved on site; more than 60 per cent concerned access to houses, 25 per cent access to roads and 10 per cent retaining and parapet walls. The report attributes the drainage problems to the designs of culverts and drains not being settled up front. It also states that no physical or economic displacement of people or resettlement impacts were experienced, and that most of the land used to widen the roads was already held by the Road Development Authority or was obtained through voluntary land donations from project beneficiaries.
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,386 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report states that the project caused no physical or economic displacement of people at all. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.outcome: The credits closed on 30 June 2015. The Inspection Panel request was not registered, and the Panel noted that the requesters keep the right to file again on new evidence. The Court of Appeal case over whether the drain is private or public, and with it whether project-financed works may proceed on the property, was unresolved when the Panel wrote on 10 November 2014, with an injunction in force. No later account of either the court case or the drainage was found.

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.confidence_note: The named requesters, the figures of 67 individuals and about eight properties, the court application number and the injunction are all taken from the Inspection Panel's own Notice of Non-Registration. The weakness is in what the documents say actually happened. The Panel found that the flooding harm alleged was not occurring at the time, so the central claim is of harm feared rather than suffered. The increased flooding for neighbours is attributed by Bank management to the requesters' own closure of the trench, not to the works. The Bank's completion report says there was no displacement and no resettlement impact. The 4,000-plus complaints about house and road access are counted by the completion report but not described, and all but two were resolved on site, so it is not known what loss, if any, people suffered. The land obtained through 'voluntary land donations from project beneficiaries' is recorded with no figure for how much land or how many donors.

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.title: Sixty-Five Squatter Families Moved into Flats at Salem, and Land Taken in Chennai
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.place: Salem city, Tamil Nadu, with land acquisition under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, India
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.point: Salem, the one town under the project's urban investment component where resettlement took place (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Salem, Tamil Nadu)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan L4798 for the Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780). US$300 million approved 5 July 2005; US$290.87 million disbursed against total project costs of US$410.5 million, compared with US$434 million at appraisal. Original closing 30 March 2011; actual closing 31 March 2014. The project was restructured in June 2009. It financed 110 sub-projects under the urban investment component as well as the Chennai urban transport sub-component, and paid rehabilitation and resettlement costs: under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, INR 191.21 million was spent to March 2014 on rehabilitation and resettlement together with shifting of utilities, against INR 137.22 million estimated at appraisal (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014; IEG ICR Review ICRR14687, 12 May 2015).

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.community: Under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders were affected, including the resettlement of five displaced families. The cost of private land acquisition and resettlement and rehabilitation assistance there was INR 132.32 million, about US$2.20 million, or 8.5 per cent of that sub-component's cost. Under the urban investment component, 110 sub-projects were carried out; private land acquisition was involved in only seven of them and resettlement in one. In all, 21 hectares of private land were acquired from 31 landowners, and about 45 hectares of government land were transferred, including 23 acres of temple land. The resettlement took place in Salem, where 65 squatter families were moved into multi-storied apartments. Total compensation and resettlement assistance for those eight sub-projects came to INR 30 million, 0.73 per cent of their cost. The completion report records instances of delays in paying compensation and resettlement assistance, later addressed after follow-up by the Bank team and the state's urban development fund. At loan closure all compensation and assistance had been paid, except that the 65 families moved into the Salem apartment had not been given title to their flats: under Tamil Nadu rules titles were to be issued in December 2014, at the end of a five-year stay. An end-term impact evaluation of the Salem families found their incomes up, because more family members were working, and their housing better, having moved from huts to built flats. The same evaluation recorded what was wrong: drinking water supply was erratic and flats on the upper floors got no water because of problems lifting it; allotment of flats took no account of the elderly, old and sick, some of whom were put on higher floors; and residents reported thefts and a lack of security. The families kept ties to where they had lived, still sending children to schools there, visiting doctors there and mostly still working there. A separate evaluation of the Chennai transport families found 75 per cent satisfied with the rate of compensation, which the report attributes to a consent award process for private land and payment for structures without depreciation; compensation money was mostly spent on improving houses, 40 per cent of it. Land availability was a running problem: about 16 of the more than 40 sites needed for urban sub-projects had to be changed, for reasons including objections from nearby residents and court cases over unclear land titles.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.displaced_label: families relocated (65 squatter families at Salem, 5 displaced families under the Chennai urban transport sub-component)
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,300 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 65 squatter families resettled at Salem and five displaced families resettled under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 70 families in all, alongside 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders affected in Chennai and 31 landowners whose land was acquired.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 March 2014 with the 65 Salem families living in the flats but without title to them, which was due in December 2014. The Bank advised Salem Corporation to act on the impact evaluation's findings and to issue the titles when due. No document found records whether the titles were issued.

sources.title: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, India Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780), ICR00003125
Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780), ICRR14687

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.confidence_note: The counts of families, landowners, hectares and the rupee amounts all come from the Bank's own completion report, which also carries the impact evaluation's findings on water, floor allotment and theft at the Salem flats. What is thin is that the impact evaluation is summarised in the completion report rather than published with it, so its sample size and method are not known, and no independent study of the Salem resettlement was found. The report does not say where in Salem the families were moved from or to.

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.title: Land and Property Taken Without Payment on an Assam Roads Package
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.place: Assam State Roads Project corridors, Assam, India
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.point: Guwahati, seat of the Assam Public Works Roads Department and the Assam State Roads Board that ran the project; the documents do not name which of the project's packages the uncompensated acquisition happened on (OpenStreetMap city point)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-81360 for the Assam State Roads Project (P096018). US$320 million approved 13 March 2012, revised commitment US$321,748,396.16 and US$284,447,922.45 disbursed. Original closing 31 March 2018; restructured at level 2 on 29 March 2018 and closed 30 September 2019, 18 months late. Total project cost US$284,447,922.45. The loan paid for resettlement and rehabilitation assistance to project-affected people alongside the road works, and the Bank suspended work on one package until compensation was paid (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020; IEG ICR Review, 26 June 2020).

lenders.name: World Bank, trust fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-11446 alongside the loan: US$1,750,000 committed, revised to US$1,748,396.16, all of it disbursed (IEG ICR Review, 26 June 2020).

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated roads in Assam, 978 km by closing against a revised target of 1,000 km. At appraisal, social screening covered about 420 km of roads, with a census and socio-economic survey of the people in every structure and on all land within the corridor of impact for Phase I of the upgrading component. The assessment concluded that widening to two lanes would not need extensive resettlement because the work would mostly stay inside the existing right of way, and that about 80 per cent of the land needed was already available in stretches along the Phase I corridors. On one of the project's packages that broke down. The completion report states plainly that the project departed from the agreements reached under the Resettlement Action Plan and that the land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners. As a corrective measure, work on the affected package was suspended until the required processes were completed and the compensation funds were transferred. The completion report says compensation was otherwise largely paid on time, 'barring for one package'. The remaining compensation payment for land acquisition is recorded as settled by the time the report was written. The project also could not obtain utilisation certificates for money spent on land acquisition and utility shifting by other state agencies, which the state met from its own funds, and the project's financial management rating was lowered to unsatisfactory for a year after it took two years to answer the Auditor General's inspection report. The policy on indigenous peoples was triggered at appraisal because some corridors were expected to pass through areas where indigenous communities had settled, and an Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared, but the completion report states the policy was never applied during implementation because the project did not pass through any major tribal settlements.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,891 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, and no document found says how many owners had their land and property taken without payment on the affected package.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2019. Work on the package where land and property had been taken without payment was suspended until the compensation was transferred, and the completion report records the outstanding land acquisition compensation as settled. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 26 June 2020 does not mention the uncompensated acquisition at all.

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.confidence_note: The statement that land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners is the Bank's own, in its completion report, and the suspension of the package is recorded there too. What is thin is everything around it: the report does not name the package, the corridor, the district or the owners, does not say how many owners there were or how long they went unpaid, and does not say how much was eventually transferred or when. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the same completion report leaves the episode out, so there is no second account of it.

_dropped_P110051_haryana_power.reason: Haryana Power System Improvement Project (P110051): no actual harm found. The completion report of 25 June 2018 and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 21 November 2018 record that all the land was government land, acquired by Haryana State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd and transferred to the transmission company, that compensation of INR 1,654,749,000 was paid for crops, forest, railway and land costs across 33 transmission sub-projects, and that three sub-projects were dropped or moved after community agitation. No relocation, no unpaid compensation, no arrests and no deaths are recorded; the two accidents noted in the completion report are not described and no injury or death is stated. ICIJ gives 3,907 for this project.

_dropped_P128966_fata_rural_roads.reason: MDTF FATA Emergency Rural Roads Project (P128966): no actual harm found. The completion report of 18 May 2016 and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 28 February 2017 record that all land procured was agricultural, that no residential land was taken and no resettlement was needed, that compensation claims were processed and paid, and that affected people expressed general satisfaction, with a few landowners saying the rates should have been higher given inflation. No count of affected people, no relocation, no unpaid compensation, no arrests and no deaths tied to the project are recorded. The project did fail to comply with the Bank's environmental safeguards, with almost no mitigation measures implemented at the sites and no environmental monitoring, but no harm to identifiable people is recorded from that. ICIJ gives 3,829 for this project.
